analysis.one_liner: Bans all oil, gas, and mineral leasing in the Arctic Ocean.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 12 senators, never received a committee hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the law governing offshore waters to bar the Interior Department from ever issuing or renewing a lease for oil, gas, or mineral exploration or production in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas [S2][S3]. Its findings say Arctic drilling is incompatible with avoiding the worst effects of climate change and would threaten fisheries, migratory birds, and Indigenous communities that depend on the Arctic [S3]. It was introduced in May 2017 and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where no further action was ever taken [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who bear the costs of climate change, coastal communities, commercial fishing interests, and Alaska Native communities that rely on Arctic subsistence hunting and fishing; the bill's stated aim is keeping Arctic fossil fuels undeveloped [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities, fishermen, and climate-exposed publics

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Interior Department from issuing or renewing any lease or authorization for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort Sea and Chukchi Sea Planning Areas [S2][S3].
States as national policy that the Arctic Ocean should be managed in the public's interest, including by keeping fossil fuels in the ground to avoid dangerous climate impacts [S2][S3].
Its findings note the Arctic Ocean's fragile ecosystems are critical to fisheries, migratory birds, Indigenous populations, and subsistence hunters, all of which drilling would put at risk [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to a potential drilling frontier, and Alaska officials would forgo possible future energy jobs and federal revenue from Arctic offshore development — though no production was underway in these waters at the time, and the area had proved commercially disappointing for major drillers.

drawbacks.text: The ban would permanently close an area to domestic energy development, foregoing whatever jobs, leases revenue, and oil supply Arctic production might eventually have provided — a cost that would fall partly on Alaska's economy.

A critics' argument in good faith: blocking drilling in one region does not by itself reduce world oil consumption, since oil companies can supply the same barrels elsewhere; the climate benefit depends on the global supply effect of removing Arctic reserves, which the bill's own findings assert but which is debated.
Companies and their investors holding or valuing Arctic leases would see those assets barred from development, an uncompensated loss for a legal use they had pursued for years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — avoiding the risks of Arctic oil development to the climate, fisheries, and Indigenous subsistence — is broad and, by the bill's logic, permanent. The main cost is borne by a narrow set of energy companies and Alaska's hopes for offshore revenue, in an area where exploration had repeatedly failed to find commercially viable production. The trade-off favors the public, but it forecloses rather than compensates the losing side.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill twice and sent it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on May 1, 2017, joined by 10 Democratic colleagues and one Independent, Sen. Bernie Sanders [S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources; that referral is the last recorded action on the bill [S5].
The committee never held a markup or vote, and the full Senate never considered the bill before the 115th Congress expired on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests kept Arctic Ocean waters available for potential future leasing, and the Senate Energy Committee's leadership was spared a fight over banning it. No one who supported the ban got any part of it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas interests and the committee's leadership

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban Arctic Ocean oil and gas leasing.

for.name: 11 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 12 total Senate supporters.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 12 supporters was a Democrat or Independent, and no Republican signed on; the Republican-led committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Oil and gas exploration and production companies
industries.note: The bill would permanently bar these companies from leasing and drilling in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas. They had pursued Arctic offshore exploration for years; the ban would extinguish that opportunity and any future production revenue.

industries.industry: Commercial fishing and Alaska Native subsistence economies
industries.note: The bill's findings describe Arctic ecosystems critical to fisheries and subsistence hunting that drilling would risk; keeping the ocean unleased protects those livelihoods alongside the public's climate interest.
